commonsFile: File:Qadisha Valley, Aerial View From Qannoubine Monastery.jpg
attribution: Evan Williams — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
location: Qadisha (Holy) Valley, Bsharri district, north Lebanon
alt: The deep Qadisha gorge seen from the Qannoubine Monastery area, with terraced slopes falling toward the valley floor.
caption: The gorge cut into Mount Lebanon where Maronite hermits and monasteries have clung to the cliffs for centuries; it is the walking heart of the concept, and in February snow lies on the upper rim.

commonsFile: File:Cedars of God (Lebanon cedar forests), Lebanon.jpg
attribution: © Vyacheslav Argenberg / http://www.vascoplanet.com/ — CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
location: Cedars of God, above Bsharri, Mount Lebanon
alt: Ancient Lebanon cedars in the protected grove high above Bsharri.
caption: The surviving high-altitude cedar grove above the Qadisha Valley; in February to March it is typically snow-covered, making the road up and any walking weather-dependent.

attribution: © Vyacheslav Argenberg / http://www.vascoplanet.com/ — CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: Columns and cella wall of the Roman Temple of Bacchus at Baalbek.
caption: The best-preserved of Baalbek's Roman temples, in the Bekaa Valley. Baalbek lies in a governorate where UK advice is against all but essential travel, which is part of why this concept is excluded.

attribution: Bdx — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: The Crusader castle at Byblos, built of Roman and earlier stone, beside the ancient harbour town.
caption: Byblos is among the oldest continuously inhabited ports on the Mediterranean and the route's gentlest stop, a first night north of Beirut for souk walks, seafood and the excavated Phoenician town.

attribution: Dennis Chanter — CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
location: Jeita Grotto, Nahr al-Kalb valley, Lebanon
alt: Illuminated limestone formations inside the Jeita Grotto north of Beirut.
caption: Two linked karst caves with an underground river and some of the longest known stalactites; a short half-day from Beirut that adds a geological chapter to the culture-heavy route.

commonsFile: File:Pigeon Rocks of Beirut, Rock of Raouche, Beirut, Lebanon.jpg
attribution: © Vyacheslav Argenberg / http://www.vascoplanet.com/ — CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: The Raouche sea stacks off Beirut's western corniche.
caption: Beirut's best-known landmark and the start of the corniche walk; a free, easy introduction to a city of cafes, bakeries and the rebuilt downtown.

attribution: © Vyacheslav Argenberg / https://www.vascoplanet.com/ — CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: The Crusader Sea Castle on its causeway at Sidon, with the fishing harbour behind.
caption: Sidon's medieval castle and soap-museum old town are the southern coast's highlight, but the whole South governorate is under advice against all travel, so it is shown here only as an idea.

attribution: © Vyacheslav Argenberg — CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: The courtyard and arcades of the Great Mosque of Damascus.
caption: One of the oldest monumental mosques in the world and the centre of Damascus's old city; a day here with the souks and Christian quarter is the core of the Syrian chapter.

commonsFile: File:Krak des Chevaliers Castle, Inner and outer walls, Syria.jpg
attribution: © Vyacheslav Argenberg — CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
location: Krak des Chevaliers, Homs governorate, Syria
alt: Concentric inner and outer walls of the Crusader castle on its hilltop.
caption: The finest surviving Crusader fortress, between the Syrian coast and the Orontes valley; included here as geography and heritage only, since Syria is under advice against all travel.

commonsFile: File:Palmyra, Syria, Colonnade and Temple of Bel.jpg
attribution: © Vyacheslav Argenberg — CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: The Great Colonnade with the Temple of Bel behind, photographed before the 2015 destruction of the temple.
caption: The caravan city in the Syrian desert; the Temple of Bel and other monuments were deliberately destroyed by ISIS in 2015, so this image shows what the site looked like before the war damage.

attribution: Bernard Gagnon — CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: A tower and fortifications of the Aleppo Citadel above the old city.
caption: The citadel anchors Aleppo's medieval city of souks, khans and mosques, much of it damaged in the 2012-2016 battle; this photograph was taken before the war and is not a current view.

attribution: © Vyacheslav Argenberg — CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
location: Norias of Hama, Orontes River, Syria
alt: Giant wooden waterwheels on the Orontes River in Hama.
caption: The norias, some more than 20 m across, are Hama's emblem and an easy stop on the road between Damascus and Aleppo in a Syria-wide concept.
